stories.headline: Burberry CEO Exalts ‘Creative and Commercial Alchemy’
stories.claim: Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman outlines brand strategy, Regent Street flagship plans and a Shanghai exhibition at a WWD summit.
stories.summary: Burberry chief executive Joshua Schulman spoke at the WWD Apparel and Retail CEO Summit in New York, describing a performance culture built on what he called creative and commercial alchemy. He credited creative director Daniel Lee as a key partner and pointed to recent collaborations, including a London Fashion Week collection with textile designer Celia Birtwell and a swimwear line with Hunza G. Schulman said the Burberry Forward turnaround, launched in 2024 to reverse slumping sales, continues, with a focus on timeless British luxury. He outlined plans for the redeveloped Regent Street flagship, dubbed Burberry House, and an 'Ever Forward' exhibition in Shanghai near the Bund, both marking the brand's 170th anniversary. He acknowledged difficult market conditions but said the company remains optimistic.
key_points: Joshua Schulman, Burberry's CEO, spoke at the WWD Apparel and Retail CEO Summit in New York.
The Burberry Forward strategy, launched in 2024, aims to reverse falling sales and restore profitability by re-centring on classic British luxury.
Recent collaborations include a Celia Birtwell collection shown at London Fashion Week and a swimwear line with Hunza G.
The Regent Street flagship, Burberry House, will include a public Burberrys clock, an archive gallery and a café.
An 'Ever Forward' exhibition in Shanghai, near the Bund, is billed as the brand's largest ever and runs for a month.
Schulman gave few specifics on 2027 plans, while acknowledging challenging market conditions.
stories.market_take: Little immediate market effect; the update reinforces the Burberry Forward turnaround story.

stories.headline: A Mystery Buyer Has Spent $311 Million Assembling a 19-Acre Waterfront Estate in Naples
stories.claim: An unidentified buyer has spent $311 million assembling nearly 19 acres of Gulf-front property in Naples, Florida.

The first purchase, in 2025, was $225 million for a roughly 15-acre compound previously owned by the DeGroote family, a record for the largest residential sale in Florida. stories.headline: MarineMax Reports Fiscal 2026 Fourth Quarter and Full Year Results – Company Announcement
stories.claim: MarineMax reports fiscal Q4 and full-year 2026 results, with revenue down and gross margin up, while awaiting its takeover by Safe Harbor.
stories.summary: MarineMax, the US boat and yacht retailer and superyacht services company, reported fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of $520.1 million, down from $552.2 million a year earlier, as lower boat sales weighed. Gross margin rose to 37.4% from 34.7%, and the company posted a net loss of $13.0 million, or $0.59 per share, against a $0.9 million loss a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA rose 26% to $21.8 million. Management will hold no conference call and will give no fiscal 2027 guidance.

stories.headline: French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe
stories.claim: French national blood service says hackers raised temperatures at three cold stores, part of a wider wave of European fridge cyber-attacks.
stories.summary: France's national blood service (EFS) said hackers accessed control systems at three cold stores run by its contractors and raised temperature and defrosting thresholds to very high levels. Alarm systems let technicians act before blood products were compromised, and stored plasma and medicine were moved elsewhere. The attack followed overnight on Monday and comes amid a wave of refrigeration hacks across Europe, with supermarket fridges in almost a dozen countries reaching up to 50C and causing millions of euros of food damage. Retailers in Italy, Germany, Romania and the UK were also targeted, and a French Crédit Mutuel branch reported a cyber-attack. No group has claimed responsibility and the motive is unknown, though some experts suspect state involvement.

stories.headline: Food prices in Europe: Where are grocery costs rising fastest?
stories.claim: Eurozone food inflation is rising unevenly, with unprocessed food up sharply in October and southern Italy's lorry-driver blockade emptying shelves.
stories.summary: Eurostat's preliminary data show eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, the highest in over three years, driven mainly by energy costs up 20.8%. Food, alcohol and tobacco rose 1.6% year on year, but unprocessed food such as fruit, vegetables, meat and fish climbed 4.6%, up from 2.7% in August. Italy saw unprocessed food up 7.5%, and a two-week lorry-driver protest over diesel costs in late October emptied shelves across Campania, Puglia and Calabria. France's fresh products rose 8%, while Germany's food rose only 0.4%. Economists expect inflation to keep climbing, with Pantheon Macroeconomics forecasting a peak of 4.5% in January and a possible ECB rate rise in December.

The report points to an algorithm in the government's integrated assessment tool, which assesses home care entitlements for older Australians and has been found to routinely under-assess needs. The thinktank makes eight recommendations, including a mandatory audit and public register of all ADM use and an independent oversight body. The attorney general's department has been developing an ADM framework since consultation ended in January 2025, but no draft date has been given. An independent MP, Kate Chaney, has also introduced a private member's bill on the issue.

stories.claim: Musk's record political spending failed to help Republicans in the US midterms, and Democrats won a resounding victory.
stories.summary: Elon Musk spent almost $450m (about £334m) backing Republican candidates in the US midterm elections, more than anyone has spent in a single election cycle, yet Democrats won a decisive victory. Among the most notable results, Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton for a Texas Senate seat, despite at least $45m of Musk's money supporting Paxton, according to a BBC analysis of campaign finance data. Musk seemed to concede by joking on X that his election-interfering space lasers had not worked, and he later stopped posting about politics. The result could bring tougher scrutiny of tech and AI firms under Democratic influence, including SpaceX, which has gained about $10bn in government contracts since Trump's election, and new limits on data centres. Tesla and SpaceX shares fell on Wednesday morning while the broader tech sector rose.
key_points: Musk spent about $450m (£334m) on Republican candidates, a record for any US election cycle.
Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, despite at least $45m of Musk's support for Paxton.
Democrats are expected to face pressure to scrutinise tech firms, with some lawmakers calling for investigations into SpaceX's government role.
Several US states passed measures limiting data centre development, and the new Georgia governor campaigned partly on curbing them.
Tesla fell about 4.9% and SpaceX about 3.4% on Wednesday morning while tech stocks broadly rose.
SpaceX has not yet commented publicly on Musk's spending and posts, according to the BBC.
stories.market_take: Tesla and SpaceX face possible regulatory scrutiny and political uncertainty, which could weigh on sentiment toward Musk-linked stocks.

stocks.reason: Shares fell on Wednesday and Musk-linked political and regulatory risk may weigh on sentiment.

stories.headline: Scare campaigns: Victoria’s major parties trade blows over AI-generated videos of leaders in election ads
stories.claim: Victorian parties in Australia are trading AI-generated deepfake election ads, prompting calls for a ban and tighter rules.
stories.summary: In the run-up to the Victorian state election in Australia, the Labor and Liberal parties have both used AI-generated videos of their leaders in campaign material. A Labor video showed Liberal leader Jess Wilson with a fabricated voice warning of US-style healthcare costs, which her party called garbage. The Liberals have posted AI videos of Premier Ben Carroll asleep at his desk. A conservative lobby group, Advance Australia, also released an AI video depicting a fake Labor victory. Experts and the Greens are calling for AI in political ads to be banned, and Transparency International Australia says trust in politicians is at an all-time low. South Australia already bans deepfakes that show people doing things they did not do without consent, with fines of up to A$5,000.
key_points: Labor released an AI-generated video of Liberal leader Jess Wilson warning about US-style healthcare costs.
The Liberal Party has posted AI videos of Premier Ben Carroll asleep at his desk.

stories.headline: After the midterms, a bigger clash over data centers could be coming
stories.claim: US midterm results give Democrats control of Congress, raising prospects for limits on AI data centres.
stories.summary: Following the 3 November US midterm elections, which gave Democrats control of Congress while Republicans hold the White House, TechCrunch reports that anger over AI data centres became a political issue. An NBC exit poll found almost 80% of respondents opposed data centres being built in their neighbourhoods, and almost 60% said they were a crucial or major factor in their vote. Local ballot measures and candidates opposing data centres won in several states, including Ohio, Texas and Michigan. Likely next steps include construction moratoriums and rules requiring data centres to pay for grid upgrades. Goldman Sachs predicts construction delays in Georgia and Texas, though any federal bill could face a veto.

stories.headline: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
stories.claim: Hackers disrupted freezers storing blood in France and supermarket freezers across Europe; culprits remain unidentified.
stories.summary: French authorities said cold rooms storing blood at the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by hackers who tried to raise temperatures, but staff intervened and no blood products were lost. The attacks follow similar freezer hacks on supermarkets in seven European countries, and freezers at least six US military bases were reportedly defrosted in August. Researchers at several firms, including Sekoia, Lupovis and Previdian, are studying honeypot data and suggest coordination, but attribution is unclear. Possible suspects include Russian hacktivists, Iranian-aligned actors, nation-state groups or teenagers. Russian group NoName057(16) claimed the attack but Sekoia is sceptical.

stories.summary: DW reports that large AI-related bond sales by US tech giants are competing with European governments and companies for investment capital. Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle have issued about $250 billion in dollar bonds since the start of 2025, plus €37 billion in euro bonds, with Microsoft recently adding a $25 billion sale. ECB economists and an OECD study are cited as warning of wider financing pressures in Europe.

The ECB has warned that concentrated debt inflows could make it harder for other firms and sectors to borrow.

stories.headline: AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
stories.claim: Geoffrey Hinton warns AI could trigger a major incident within a year or two and says humanity might have been better off never developing it.
stories.summary: Nobel-winning AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton told the Guardian that AI could cause a large-scale incident, such as a temporary power or financial system blackout, later this year or next. He said humanity might have been better off never developing the technology, though he remains hopeful it can be managed. Hinton criticised leaders of major AI firms, saying he did not trust OpenAI's Sam Altman and suggesting Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk prioritise money over risk. He backed mandatory independent testing of frontier AI models, similar to the US FDA drug approval process, as featured in a new documentary about AI risks.
key_points: Hinton, 78, says AI could trigger a Chornobyl-style event, such as an AI-enabled attack causing a brownout or a week-long financial system shutdown.
He said it might turn out humans would have been better off never developing AI, but described AI as having the potential for a wonderful future.
He called for mandatory pre-release testing of frontier AI models, citing the thalidomide drug scandal as a warning against releasing first and suing later.
He said he did not trust Sam Altman at all and criticised Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk for prioritising money over risk.
Comments came ahead of a screening of the documentary AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About, featuring Hinton and Demis Hassabis.
The UK government plans to seek global AI principles during its G20 presidency next year, while the US has said it wants AI companies to regulate themselves.

stories.headline: Google Is Forcing Schools to Choose Between Its Search Engine and AI
stories.claim: Google will switch off its AI products for K-12 student accounts by default, and blocking AI also blocks Google Search for students.
stories.summary: Google said on Tuesday that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search AI features will be off by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators opt in. The company also said that if schools keep AI disabled, students will not be able to access Google Search. The change reverses an August decision that had automatically enabled AI in Google Classroom. The move follows an October open letter from tech and child-safety groups urging districts to disable Gemini. Google said schools can switch Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search on individually, and it is piloting a Guided Learning tool at select US schools. New York City's mayor Zohran Mamdani criticised the move as an abuse of Google's monopoly power, while the Los Angeles Unified School District said it is reviewing the announcement.
key_points: Google will turn off its AI products by default for K-12 student accounts, so administrators must opt in.
Schools that keep AI off will also lose access to Google Search for students, according to Google.

Revenue reached a record $13.4 billion, with data center contributing $8.5 billion, about 63% of the total. AMD forecasts next-quarter revenue of $17 billion and expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. The CFO said data center could exceed 80% of total revenue. Gaming revenue fell 40% year on year to $773 million as component price rises and shortages, driven by AI data centre demand, slowed consumer sales. CEO Lisa Su said AMD is planning for a down year for its consumer markets in 2027.

Data center revenue was $8.5 billion, roughly 63% of total revenue.
AMD guided to about $17 billion of revenue next quarter and more than 80% growth in 2027.
Gaming revenue fell 40% year on year to $773 million.
Shortages and price rises in RAM and components are hitting consumer PC and console sales.
Lisa Su said AMD is planning for a down year in consumer markets in 2027.
stories.market_take: Strong data centre guidance supports AMD shares, while the weaker consumer outlook and component shortages are a warning for PC and console makers.

stories.headline: GSMA warns of growing risks to mobile networks from extreme weather
stories.claim: GSMA says extreme weather costs mobile operators $1.7bn a year, possibly rising above $3bn by 2050, and urges coordinated resilience.
stories.summary: The GSMA, the global mobile industry body, has published a six-part research series and a policy document on how extreme weather threatens mobile networks. It estimates that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion a year to repair cell sites, a figure it expects could nearly double to more than $3 billion annually by 2050. The report identifies electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability, since networks can go offline once backup power runs out. It calls for operators, governments, regulators and energy providers to coordinate, and for policy frameworks that are outcome-based rather than prescriptive.
key_points: Severe storms and floods already cost mobile operators about $1.7 billion a year to repair cell radio sites.
The GSMA projects this could rise to more than $3 billion a year by 2050.
Power supply is identified as the biggest vulnerability, with outages possible once backup power is exhausted.
Recommendations include resilience by design, cross-sector testing and coordination among operators, utilities and emergency services.
Policy principles favour outcome-based regulation and consultation between governments and operators.
Barriers include internal data silos and differing regulatory and climate-disclosure frameworks.
stories.market_take: Mainly a policy and industry report; little direct effect on listed telecom shares.

stories.headline: Russia demands Apple hand over user phone and message records to its security agencies when requested
stories.claim: Russia's communications regulator added Apple and Microsoft to a register requiring data retention and disclosure to security agencies.
stories.summary: Russia's communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, added Apple and Microsoft to an official register of digital communication providers on 2 October 2026, according to Bloomberg. The listing obliges the companies to store customer details and communication records within Russia for three years and to provide them to authorities on request. Firms that break the rules face fines and, if violations persist, possible service bans. Google Meet, WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat and others are already on the register. Apple has faced a series of disputes with Russia, including restrictions on App Store payments, removal of apps and an antitrust case over preinstalling state-backed software. Neither company has publicly said how it will respond.

stories.headline: What would freedom of movement mean for the UK in 2026?
stories.claim: Explainer on what a return to EU freedom of movement could mean for the UK, amid speculation about a deal ahead of a summit.
stories.summary: The Independent sets out what a return to UK-EU freedom of movement could mean, as speculation grows that a deal could be struck before an international summit later this month. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called for an honest discussion on migration since Brexit but denies planning to propose free movement at the talks, and has said any return would need a referendum and would likely wait until after the next general election, due by 2029. The piece explains the likely effects: an end to the points-based system for EU nationals, the removal of the 90-day Schengen limit for Britons, and reciprocal healthcare and pension rights. It also notes that net migration peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023 before falling to around 171,000 after tighter visa rules, and that smaller youth mobility schemes remain under discussion.
key_points: Speculation is growing that the UK could strike a freedom of movement deal with the EU before a summit later this month.

Any return to free movement would require a referendum and is unlikely before the next general election, due by 2029.
Free movement would end the points-based system for EU nationals and remove visa and sponsorship requirements for Britons travelling to Europe.
Net migration peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023 and fell to around 171,000 after visa tightening in 2024 and 2025.
Smaller targeted mobility deals, including a proposed two-way youth scheme for ages 18 to 30, reportedly remain on the table.

stories.headline: Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds
stories.claim: A Stanford study finds 44% of widely cited LLM research claims have expired as newer models outpace earlier findings.
stories.summary: Stanford researchers Owen Queen and James Zou tested 50 widely cited claims about large language models against 20 models released between July 2024 and September 2026. They found 44% of the claims had expired, and the 22 findings with an estimated expiry lasted an average of 15.7 months. Claims about what models cannot do expire fastest, including known weaknesses such as counting letters or losing information in long contexts. Findings about preferences and tendencies, such as political bias and sycophancy, have proven more durable. Citation fabrication has fallen sharply in some models, but one 2026 model still fabricated 69% of references. The researchers urge papers to document the specific model, version and date, and to publish prompts and code so results can be re-tested.

The case was brought by Hungarian website operator Like Company. Opinions of the advocate general are not binding but are usually followed by judges.

stories.headline: Why Rolex, Audemars Piguet, and Patek Philippe Dominate the $26.6 Billion Secondary Watch Market

stories.summary: A 53-page Secondary Market Report 2026 by Oliver R. Müller of LuxeConsult values the pre-owned watch market at a conservative 22 billion Swiss francs (about $26.6 billion), growing 8 to 11 percent a year. Three brands, Rolex, Audemars Piguet and Patek Philippe, account for more than 60 percent of secondary transactional value. Audemars Piguet has just launched its own certified pre-owned (CPO) programme, following Rolex's CPO, which is expected to reach close to 1 billion Swiss francs in transaction value by year end. Müller predicts secondary sales will overtake primary sales between 2034 and 2038, driven largely by younger buyers.

stories.headline: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
stories.claim: Supermarkets across Europe were hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting connected fridges and freezers, raising device security concerns.
stories.summary: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their connected fridges and freezers, prompting questions about the security of internet-connected equipment. Experts say there is no evidence that domestic appliances were targeted in these attacks. The UK's NCSC is working with international partners and said it was unaware of any impact in the UK. Researchers found more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces linked to British retailers that can be reached over the public internet, which does not necessarily mean they can be hacked. The article also recalls the 2025 ransomware attacks on M&S and the Co-op, which led to empty shelves. Experts say retailers must clarify who is responsible for securing equipment.

stories.headline: A hidden network of nudifying tools was found lurking inside harmless looking AI apps
stories.claim: Wired investigation finds hundreds of disguised apps on Google and Apple stores secretly offered AI nudifying deepfake tools.
stories.summary: A Wired investigation, with researchers from AI Forensics, found hundreds of apps on Google Play and Apple's App Store that presented as harmless tools such as pet photo editors or workout coaches. A server-side mechanism reportedly switched some users to a hidden interface that generated sexual deepfakes, with a network of more than 400 connected apps and domains. Users could buy digital currency for the features, and the apps were reportedly promoted through deceptive ads on Meta's platforms. Wired traced much of the network to Chinese developers and a Hong Kong firm, KeLing Technology Limited. Google removed one popular app with over 100,000 downloads and Apple removed 19 more. The EU's ban on nudifier apps takes effect in about one month.

Apps appeared as pet editors, language tutors and workout coaches on both app stores.
A server decided whether users saw the harmless or hidden version.
Ads reportedly ran on Meta's platforms, and some payments went through Apple Pay and Google Pay.

The EU ban on nudifier apps takes effect in about a month.

stories.headline: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
stories.claim: Trump's executive order renaming AI as Super Intelligence is spreading unevenly across government and tech firms.
stories.summary: An MIT Technology Review analysis looks at how the late-September executive order, which asked federal agencies to rename artificial intelligence as Super Intelligence, is being applied. Some agencies, such as ICE and the NIH, have adopted the term, while the Pentagon and HHS have not consistently used it. Trump criticised the Wall Street Journal on October 27 for not using the term. Among tech leaders who signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, the language is mixed: Zuckerberg and Musk use it most, while Google, Microsoft and Amazon executives mostly still say AI. The order requires agencies to draft a new legislative definition by the end of October.

Some agencies, including ICE and the NIH, use the new term while others, such as the Pentagon, have not.
